lead: A cloud service looks like a website until you take it apart. Taken apart, it is a stack of four layers: physical hardware at the bottom, virtualisation above it, a platform above that, and the application on top. Three bands cut across all four: security, management and governance. This stack is the structure half of the cloud reference model. It says where each part lives and who controls it — provider at the bottom, consumer at the top.
prereq: You need: Chapter 1.3 for the five essential characteristics and Chapter 1.4 for the cost-and-control trade-off.

blocks.text: Read the layers from the bottom, because each one is built on the one below it.

Physical layer. Data centres: buildings with power, cooling and racks. Inside are servers (CPU and RAM), storage devices (hard disk, SSD) and network equipment (switches, routers, links to the internet). These are fixed, owned, physical assets. Whoever owns them owns the bottom of the model.

Virtualisation layer. A hypervisor runs on a physical server and carves it into virtual machines (VMs). Each VM gets a virtual CPU, memory and disk, and cannot see the other VMs. Software-defined networking does the same to switches. This layer is what makes pooling possible: a spare slice of one server becomes a VM for a different customer.

Platform layer. Operating system, runtime (Java, Python, Node.js), middleware and databases. A VM with an OS installed sits at the top of virtualisation and the bottom of the platform. A managed database service belongs here: the provider patches it and takes backups.
Application layer. The software a person actually opens — a college portal, a UPI app, a video player.

Control shifts as you move up. The provider controls the physical and virtualisation layers and very little of the application layer. The consumer controls the application and, when buying bare infrastructure, the platform too. Chapter 1.6 shows that IaaS, PaaS and SaaS are this same stack cut at three heights.

sections.h3: Three bands that cut across every layer

blocks.text: Security, management and governance are not layers. They apply at every layer, from the server room to the web page.

Security means confidentiality, integrity, availability, authentication and isolation. Physical layer: locked racks, guards, safe disk disposal. Virtualisation layer: hypervisor hardening, so that one VM cannot read another VM's memory. Platform layer: patching and key management. Application layer: login and access control, plus denial-of-service protection so the service stays available. A gap at any one layer is a gap in the whole system; Unit 6 covers this fully.
Management is the day-to-day running of the stack:

items: Resource management: provisioning VMs, allocating CPU and memory, scheduling jobs.
Service management: deployment, monitoring, scaling, load balancing, fault recovery.
SLA management: measuring uptime and response time against the agreement, and turning the meter into a bill.

blocks.text: Governance is the set of rules written down before any of that starts: where data may be stored, who may read it, which standards apply, how long it is kept, who audits. Governance decides what management is allowed to do.

Management and security both need a live view of the same resources, which is why they are drawn as vertical bands through the stack and not as boxes on top of it. Draw all four layers and all three bands. Four layers alone is half the answer.

The reference model has two halves. The first is the layered architecture above. The second is the actor view: the named roles — consumer, provider, broker, auditor, carrier — and the boundaries between them. That is Chapter 1.8. Keep the halves separate. If a question asks for the architecture, draw the layers and the bands. If it asks for roles, draw the actors.
The layered half works as a placement test. Take any item in a cloud design and ask two questions: which layer does it live in, and who manages it?

items: Is it metal, disk or cable? Physical layer, provider-managed.
Is it a VM, virtual disk or virtual network cut from a shared pool? Virtualisation layer; the provider runs the hypervisor, the consumer runs what is inside.
Is it an OS, runtime, middleware or managed database? Platform layer.
Is it what a user clicks? Application layer.
Does security, management or governance touch it? For any real item, yes.

blocks.text: Some syllabi call this stack the 'cloud computing architectural framework'. Some call it the 'cloud computing reference model'. The diagram is the same either way.

figure.caption: The four layers, top first. Control passes from the consumer near the top to the provider near the bottom; the highlighted top layer is the one the consumer always controls, and in IaaS the consumer also builds the platform inside the VMs.

spec.aria: A four-layer stack running from the application at the top down to physical servers at the bottom, with control passing from the consumer near the top to the provider near the bottom.

examples.question: A college runs its student portal on cloud infrastructure bought as infrastructure as a service. The design has 4 virtual machines, each with 4 vCPU and 8 GB RAM, behind 1 load balancer. It also has a managed database of 200 GB and 500 GB of object storage for lecture videos. (a) Count the items in the design. (b) Find total vCPU, total RAM and total storage. (c) Place every item on the four-layer model and state who manages it. (d) Name the bands that apply.
steps: Count the items: 4 VMs + 1 load balancer + 1 managed database + 1 object store = 7 items.
Total vCPU = 4 VMs × 4 vCPU per VM = 16 vCPU.
Total RAM = 4 VMs × 8 GB per VM = 32 GB.
Total storage = 200 GB database + 500 GB object storage = 700 GB.

Virtualisation layer: the 4 VMs sit at the virtualisation layer and the college installs and patches their guest operating systems; the load balancer is also a virtualisation-layer service, but the provider runs and patches it.
Platform layer: the managed database. The provider handles patching, backup and failover; the college owns the schema and the data itself.

Virtualisation layer: the 500 GB object store. The provider's raw disks are physical-layer hardware, but the bucket the college buys is a pooled, virtualised storage resource that the provider manages; the college never touches the disks.
Application layer: the portal software the student opens in a browser.
Bands: security, management and governance apply to all 7 items, not to one layer only.
examples.answer: 7 items, holding 16 vCPU, 32 GB RAM and 700 GB storage; VMs, load balancer and object storage at the virtualisation layer, database at the platform layer, with security, management and governance across all of them.

traps: Drawing only the four layers and leaving out the security and management bands. Half the marks go with them.
Confusing the layered architecture with the actor view. Consumer, provider, broker, auditor and carrier belong to the reference model's role half, not to the layer diagram.
Putting the hypervisor in the platform layer. It belongs to virtualisation, below the operating system.
Thinking a managed database moves data responsibility to the provider. Patching moves; the data, the schema and the access rules stay with the consumer.
Treating object storage as an application feature. It is a virtualisation-layer resource: the provider pools physical disks and presents them to you as buckets, so you never touch the disks.

quiz.q: List the four layers of the cloud layered architecture, from bottom to top.
Name the three cross-cutting concerns drawn as vertical bands through the stack.
Why is the hypervisor placed in the virtualisation layer and not in the platform layer?
quiz.a: The hypervisor runs directly on physical hardware and creates the virtual machines. The operating system runs inside a VM, so it sits above the hypervisor. Anything the hypervisor manages is below any OS.

quiz.q: Why are security and management drawn as vertical bands instead of as layers on top of the stack?
quiz.a: Because they act at every layer at once: rack locks and VM isolation and OS patching and login are all security, and each belongs to a different layer. A horizontal layer would wrongly suggest they sit at one height.

quiz.q: A design has 6 VMs, each with 2 vCPU and 4 GB RAM, plus a 300 GB managed database and 100 GB of object storage. Give the item count, total vCPU, total RAM and total storage.
quiz.a: Items = 6 + 1 + 1 = 8. vCPU = 6 × 2 = 12 vCPU. RAM = 6 × 4 = 24 GB. Storage = 300 + 100 = 400 GB.

quiz.q: Place these four items on the layer model: a hypervisor, an online exam application, a Java runtime, a virtual network switch.
quiz.a: Hypervisor and virtual network switch: virtualisation layer. Java runtime: platform layer. Online exam application: application layer. Security, management and governance apply to all four.

quiz.q: A college buys IaaS but then asks the provider to patch the guest operating system as well. What happens to the boundary in the layer model, and which service model does this become?
quiz.a: Patching the guest OS moves the management boundary up from the top of virtualisation to the top of the guest OS — a managed-OS add-on on top of IaaS. The offering becomes PaaS only when the provider also supplies and runs the runtime and middleware, leaving the college the application and its data.

quiz.q: Give one reason governance can override a management decision, with an example.
quiz.a: Governance sets the rules management must obey. Example: management wants to shift load to a cheaper region, but governance says student data must stay inside the country, so the scaling plan is rejected or restricted to allowed regions.

beyond: Not for the exam. Industry architecture frameworks — the AWS Well-Architected Framework, the Azure Architecture Center, and enterprise frameworks such as TOGAF and ITIL — all reorganise this same four-layer stack plus cross-cutting bands, with more pillars and more checklists. NIST publishes a formal cloud computing reference architecture that separates the layered view from the actor view, and most later diagrams copy its split. Cloud-native designs add a container scheduling layer (Kubernetes) above the operating system, inside the platform layer, which is why newer diagrams show five layers instead of four. Search next for 'cloud computing reference model layered architecture' and 'cloud reference architecture actors'.
